name: Beth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Morrows at Hollins Farm, up the valley road past the chapel. It's mostly sheep, about five hundred ewes, a few beef cattle and some oats for feed. I do the morning feed and check the in-lamb ewes, clean water troughs, muck out the calf pens, and help Mr Morrow with whatever he's doing, gathering or dosing or fencing. I'm slow with the dogs still; they listen to him and treat me like a visitor. I love it when the work's done and you can see it, a clean pen, a full rack.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to work at Hollins?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was home with the children for years and helped run the chapel café on Saturdays. When Joseph started school, Mrs Morrow asked at chapel if anyone wanted farm work, and I put my hand up. That was three years ago. My husband Dale drives a milk tanker, collecting from the dairies all round the valley. We've got Hannah, who's twelve, and Joseph, nine. I don't use any of these AI things. I don't trust them, and I don't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get carried away with whatever's new, and then it all settles down. I'd say that after chapel, over a cup of tea, not on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing, and thank the Lord for that. I'm still learning the work, and I'd like to get it right. I don't want the ground moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Ask Mr Morrow to let me work the young dog, Fly, so she gets used to me. Keep putting a bit by from my wage every month, like we do for Hannah's school trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you about Hollins, if AI fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices for lambs, and whether the Morrows' son wants to take the farm on. If he doesn't, they might sell, and then where am I? I'm more worried about a young man not wanting to farm than about any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at home you'd keep an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dale's tanker, maybe. They're always talking about lorries driving themselves. But I've seen the lanes he drives, and I'd like to see a computer back a tanker up the Pritchards' yard in the snow.

S0.say: She'd say she's not surprised, because people get carried away with new things and then it all settles. She'd say it after chapel, not online.
S0.think: She keeps doing what she's doing and is grateful for it. She's still learning and doesn't want the ground moving under her.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and asks the farmer to let her work the young dog so it gets used to her. Keeps putting a bit of her wage aside every month as they do now.
S0.quote: I'm more worried about a young man not wanting to farm than about any computer.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's world is close-knit: chapel, the Morrows, her husband's tanker route. Her real worry is succession, whether the farmer's son will take over. She has a firm distrust of AI and confidence in local know-how, like backing a tanker up a snowy yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people pushing this have never done a day's work outside. I'd say we should look after our own, the families and the farms, and not wait for the government. I'd say it at chapel and at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry. Mr Morrow's not one for gadgets, but his son is. If they get robot dogs or those drones for gathering, they'd not need me for that. I'd still have the mucking out, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and work harder, so they'd not want to lose me. I'd keep saving a bit more, maybe stop the takeaway on Fridays. I'd not go learning computers, that's for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the weather's turning and you've not got the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned robot dogs. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's not the same. A robot sheepdog's not a dog. It doesn't lie by the fire, and it doesn't miss you when you're poorly. I'd find that sad, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the Morrows did buy the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd get on with what's left. There's always mucking out. Someone's got to do the jobs nobody wants, and I don't mind them.

S1.say: She'd say the people pushing this have never worked outside, and that communities should look after their own families and farms without waiting for government.
S1.think: She'd worry that the farmer's son would bring in robot dogs or drones for gathering, leaving her only the mucking out.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works harder so the farm won't want to lose her. Saves a bit more by stopping Friday takeaways and doesn't learn computers.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather turning before the hay is in.
S1.quote: A robot sheepdog's not a dog. It doesn't lie by the fire, and it doesn't miss you when you're poorly.
S1.fieldNote: Beth answers change by working harder and staying useful, not by learning new skills. Her sadness at a robot sheepdog is about companionship and care, not just jobs. Her view that families and communities should look after their own is firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now we come to the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing God, and we'll pay for it. I'd say families and churches need to pull together, because the government won't know what it's doing. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job, and Dale would lose his. A tanker that drives itself and a farm that runs itself, that's both of us. We've got maybe four months saved, and a mortgage. I don't know how we'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything back to the bone, straight away: no school trips, no new shoes unless they're needed, sell Dale's motorbike. I'd ask at chapel who's struggling and who can help, and we'd share, food and lifts and childcare. I'd ask my brother about the spare room at his place if it came to the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be praying a lot, and I'd still be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah and Joseph?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's twelve, she'd understand. Joseph's nine. I'd tell them God's not finished with us, and then I'd go out to the pens so they don't see me cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you turn to the government for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't. I'd not want a handout. But I'd take help from people I know, that's different, that's neighbours. If the government gave every family something, though, I suppose I'd have to take it. I'd not like it.

S2.say: She'd call it people playing God and say families and churches must pull together because the government won't know what it's doing.
S2.think: She'd lose her job and her husband would lose his, with about four months saved and a mortgage. She doesn't know how they'd manage.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone immediately, dropping school trips and selling her husband's motorbike. Organises sharing of food, lifts and childcare through chapel, and asks her brother about his spare room if they lost the house.
S2.feel: Frightened, praying a lot and still frightened.
S2.quote: I'd tell them God's not finished with us, and then I'd go out to the pens so they don't see me cry.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI takes both incomes in Beth's house at once, and she has no wish to retrain. She'd lean on church and family rather than the state, though she'd reluctantly accept government help if everyone got it. The image of going out to the pens to cry was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready, and families should start now. Pay off debts, grow some of your own food, look after each other. I'd say it at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years doesn't change much for me. I'd still lose my job at the end of it, and Dale his. I'm not going to become something else at forty-eight. But we'd be readier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pay off the car loan in the first year and put everything else by. I'd ask Mr Morrow if we could keep a few sheep and some hens on his rough ground, so we've got food of our own. And I'd talk to Hannah about what she wants to do, steer her towards nursing or teaching, where people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as two years, but it'd sit on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned faith earlier. Does it change how you'd plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. That's what I believe, but I'd not let it stop me getting ready. My mother always said, pray for rain but mend the gutter. So we'd do both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother, I suppose, and Dale's parents. And the chapel. We'd look after them as well, it goes both ways.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready and families should start now: pay off debts, grow food, look after each other.
S3.think: Five years doesn't change much for her: she'd still lose her job, and she won't become something else at 48. But they'd be readier.
S3.do: Pays off the car loan in the first year and saves everything else. Asks the farmer for rough ground to keep a few sheep and hens for food, and steers her daughter towards nursing or teaching.
S3.feel: Anxious; less than with two years, but it would sit on her.
S3.quote: My mother always said, pray for rain but mend the gutter.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change Beth's end point, but it lets her prepare in her own way: clearing debt, growing food and guiding her daughter towards caring work. Her mother's saying about praying for rain but mending the gutter sums up her faith and practicality.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and they've been wrong before. I'd not go on about it. I'd say what I always say, look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure I'd believe it. They said we'd all have flying cars. If it's ten years away, I'd carry on and see, and the children would be grown by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Hollins, keep saving what we can, and overpay the mortgage when we've got a good month. I'd wait and see if it's really coming before I upset everything. Maybe keep a few hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It'd be at the back of my mind, but I'd get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You took the two-year picture very seriously. Why not this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. Two years scared me, ten years I'd shrug off. You can't spend ten years worrying about the weather, you'd never get the washing out. I know that's not really an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most, ten years on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Joseph, he'd be nineteen. I'd want him to have a trade, or a job with people. I'd not want him sitting at home with nothing to do.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long way off and forecasters have been wrong before. She wouldn't go on about it, just tell people to look after their own.
S4.think: She's not sure she'd believe it, and her children would be grown by then anyway, so she'd carry on and see.
S4.do: Carries on at the farm, saves what she can and overpays the mortgage in good months. Waits to see if it's really coming before changing anything, and might keep a few hens.
S4.feel: Uneasy, at the back of her mind while she gets on with things.
S4.quote: You can't spend ten years worrying about the weather, you'd never get the washing out.
S4.fieldNote: Beth discounts a distant threat, and she admitted it when the contrast with the two-year picture was pointed out. Her resistance to change shows as waiting rather than denial. Her worry shifts to her son having a trade and a purpose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Dale and me both gone at once, and no time to put anything by. What would help is work, honestly, not a handout. Apprenticeships for people like Joseph, and the farms kept in families instead of bought up by big companies with robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the chapel, and I think it matters. When the mill closed in my dad's day, it was the chapel that fed people, not the government. I'd want people to remember that before they decide what we need.

headlineQuote: When the mill closed in my dad's day, it was the chapel that fed people, not the government.
portrait: Beth Petrov is 43, a newer hand on a sheep and oats farm up a valley road, who came to farm work three years ago after years at home and running the chapel café. She's traditional, churchgoing and wary of AI, which she has never used. She stays calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, worrying more about farm succession than computers, and responds by working harder. AGI in 2 years alarms her because her husband's tanker driving would go too, and she'd turn to chapel and family rather than the state. With 5 years she prepares by clearing debt and growing food; at 10 years she shrugs it off and waits to see.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband would both lose their jobs at once with no time to put anything by.
whatWouldHelp: Work rather than handouts: apprenticeships for young people like her son, and farms kept in families instead of being bought by big companies with robots.
